title: Batch files need to set the working directory
excerpt: Explorer launches programs with the program folder as the current directory, while a batch file may not, causing missing files.
body:
When a user double-clicks MyApp.exe in Explorer, the program starts without complaint. Run the same command from a `.bat` file and an error pops up about missing files. The difference is not the way the executable is invoked; it is the *current directory* that the process inherits.

Explorer sets the new process’ current directory to the folder that contains the item being launched. A batch file inherits the directory of the command prompt that started it, which is often unrelated to the program’s location. If the program looks for ancillary files next to its executable, the mismatch causes the failure.  

Below you’ll see why Explorer behaves that way, how a batch file breaks the expectation, and a reliable fix that works in every script.

## Explorer sets the current directory to the executable’s folder

When a file is double-clicked in Explorer, the shell changes the new process’ current directory to the folder that holds the clicked item. This design dates back to early Windows versions, when many programs assumed that their supporting files lived in the same directory as the executable.

Raymond Chen illustrates the point with a hypothetical “LitWare Writer”. The program opens `ABC.LIT` and then searches for `ABC.LTC` (table of contents) and `ABC.LDC` (custom dictionary) in the *current* directory. By having Explorer set the current directory to the folder that contains `ABC.LIT`, the program finds those files without having to compute its own path.

The same rule applies when the user double-clicks the `.exe` itself: the current directory becomes the executable’s folder. The original article explains this behavior in detail: [Why a program doesn't work when run from a batch file, but works when clicked](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20261026-00/?p=112797/).

## A batch file inherits the caller’s directory

A batch file runs under `cmd.exe`. When `cmd.exe` starts a program, it passes along the *current* directory that `cmd.exe` itself is using. If the batch file resides in `C:\Scripts` and the program lives in `C:\Program Files\MyApp`, the new process starts with `C:\Scripts` as its current directory.

The source notes that the customer’s program displayed an error until the directory was changed explicitly. The error stemmed from the program trying to open files relative to its current directory, which now pointed at the script folder instead of the program folder.

## Fix the mismatch with `pushd` / `popd`

The classic remedy is to change to the program’s folder before launching it, then restore the original directory afterward. `pushd` saves the current directory on a stack and switches to a new one; `popd` restores the saved directory. This approach works for local paths and also maps network shares to temporary drive letters when needed.

```bat
pushd "C:\Program Files\MyApp"
MyApp.exe
popd
```

After `pushd`, the current directory is `C:\Program Files\MyApp`, so any relative file look-ups performed by `MyApp.exe` succeed. `popd` then returns the script to its original location, keeping the environment tidy for subsequent commands. The article confirms that the customer solved the issue exactly this way.

### Why not just use `cd`?

A simple `cd` could change the directory, but it would lose the original location unless the script stored it manually. `pushd`/`popd` handle the bookkeeping automatically and are safe even if the script later changes directories again.

## When the problem surfaces

The mismatch appears most often in these scenarios:

1. Launching shortcuts from a batch file, the shortcut points to an executable, but the script runs the target with the script’s directory as current.  
2. Full-path invocation, using `C:\Program Files\MyApp\MyApp.exe` without changing directories leaves the current directory unchanged.  
3. Programs that load side-by-side DLLs, some DLLs are searched relative to the current directory, so a wrong directory can cause load failures.  
4. Tools that read configuration files, many command-line utilities read `config.ini` from the current directory; a batch file may point them at the wrong folder.  
5. Legacy applications, older code often assumes the current directory is the executable’s folder, a pattern that modern installers still rely on.

Addressing any of these cases with `pushd`/`popd` eliminates the “file not found” errors without altering the program itself.

## A minimal reproducible example

Create a folder `C:\Demo` with two files:

* `demo.exe`, a tiny program that tries to open `data.txt` in the current directory and prints its contents.  
* `data.txt`, a text file containing “Hello from Demo”.

Now write a batch file `run.bat` in `C:\Scripts`:

```bat
@echo off
"C:\Demo\demo.exe"
```

Running `run.bat` prints an error because `demo.exe` looks for `data.txt` in `C:\Scripts`. Fix it with:

```bat
@echo off
pushd "C:\Demo"
demo.exe
popd
```

The program now finds `data.txt` and prints the expected message. This mirrors the situation described in the source article.

## The takeaway

Explorer automatically sets the process’ current directory to the folder that contains the launched item; a batch file does not. When a program relies on relative paths, wrap its launch in `pushd …` / `popd` so the working directory matches the executable’s location. This small adjustment aligns batch-file behavior with Explorer and prevents “file not found” errors caused by a mismatched current directory.
